Chapter 2 Intro to R Week 3 tutorial goals: R Basics Object types Working directory Importing data R Project Exploring data .watch-out { background-color: lightpink; border: 3px solid maroon; font-weight: bold; } 2.1 RStudio What is R? What is coding? Coding is writing instructions in a computer language. There are lots of coding languages (python, html, Javascript, etc). The computer reads the code and executes the commands. R is a coding language AND “back-end” software for statistical computing. Write the R code in an R script (file). Run the code/script and the computer follows the instructions. The code is an important product! It’s not “rough work”. 2.1.1 RStudio: Integrated Development Environment (IDE) editor: R itself is very annoying and difficult to use RStudio is more user friendly, with many nice features. R studio has R do the calculations in the background Always open and use RStudio! Never R! Console Output: shows code run, (some) results, errors, etc Can write code directly here, but don’t. Have to re-type every time. Environment The environment lists saved objects Object can be many things: one number, analysis results, dataset, etc. Can “call” (use) them multiple times. Files/Plots “Files” doesn’t mean all the files on your computer. Have to tell R which folder to look at. Plots has the graphs and figures you make R Script To write code, we need an R script. Menu: File>New File>R Script Open the R script W3.R The file W3.R can be found in the folder for this class (Quercus > Files > Practical > Week 3). This R script contains all the codes I will run below. You can run them on your computers as you follow along. 2.2 Getting started A sophisticated calculator R can do whatever your calculator can do, and much more. 2 + 2 ## [1] 4 5 * 10 ## [1] 50 Ignore the ## and the number in brackets [1], they’re not really part of the output and won’t show up if you make a proper table. Objects Objects store data. Assign (create/save/change) objects using <- R does not save calculations by default! You have to put it in an object. The way to assign an object is to type object name <- data. For example, obj1 <- 15 You will see obj1 added to your environment panel. Names of objects can only contain letters, numbers, _ (underscore), or . (period), and must begin with a letter. (An Introduction to R for Research. No spaces! Functions Similar to what we did in Excel last week. Functions are what makes R useful. Lets learn two functions: c() and mean(). The function c() allows you to combine data into a single object. The function mean() allows you to calculate the mean value, similar to the AVERAGE function we used in Microsoft Excel last week. Use ?<functionname> to pull up the R documentation for the function. For example, ?c() We can use c() to combine elements, such as numbers. We can then run a function like mean() on the combined output. c(10,20) ## [1] 10 20 We assign a new object and run mean() on the new object. We called the new object “obj2”, but you could pick a different name. obj2 <- c(10,20) mean(obj2) ## [1] 15 Comments R does not evaluate lines starting with #. This allow us to add comments and explanations to the code. ?mean() # this function runs R documentation for function mean() Data types Data types tell R how the object should be read. Why do they matter? They affect what calculations can be done and how functions work. Words or labels can be specified using quotations ". These are known as characters in R. The function class() will tell you what kind of data type a variable is. Now lets create two objects, one with numbers and one with characters. numbers <- c(10,19,100) words <- c("cat ate my homework","today","100 pianos") class(numbers) ## [1] "numeric" class(words) ## [1] "character" The exact same numbers can be read as numbers or characters. The numbers 1, 2, 3 could refer to the numeric type, or they could refer to the labels “1”, “2”, “3”, which are the character type. This is sometimes a problem for students. If your code is giving an error, check the class of the object. eg1 <- c("1","3","2") mean(eg1) # characters have no mean class(eg1) ## [1] "character" We will only use numeric/integer, character, and logical (true/false) data types. Others exist, but you don’t need to know about them. Data frames To make a dataset object we use the data.frame() function. Each variable can only be one data type. If there is a mix, it will be forced to be character. scores_data <- data.frame(name = c("Besco","Anderson","Lin"), score = c(250,450,800)) View the data frame. View(scores_data) Dataframe Analysis If a dataframe has multiple variables, you need to tell the function both. dataframe first then: $ variable name Calculate the mean mean(scores_data$score) Now another mean: mean(scores_data$name) Why didn’t that work? Now lets make a plot of the data (we will learn the details later). This code is for a scatterplot: plot(x = scores_data$name, y = scores_data$score, type = "l") ## Error in `plot.window()`: ## ! need finite 'xlim' values This fails. name is a character variable, and R cannot put words on a scatterplot axis. A bar chart uses the names as labels and the scores as heights: barplot(height = scores_data$score, names.arg = scores_data$name) 2.3 Opening Data Files You can open data files by importing the dataset. There are different formats of datasets, but Comma Separated Values (csv) is the most common. Menu: File> Import Dataset > From Text (base R) Navigate to the STAR Dataset on your computer and import it Working Directories The working directory is the folder where R defaults to open and save files. Find the current working directory using the function getwd(). Change the working directory using the function setwd(““) Use getwd() after? setwd("") getwd() If the file you want is not in the current working directory, you can either: Move the file to your working directory change your working directory (Menu: Session > Set Working Directory > Choose Directory, and select the folder where the file is located) Advanced move: if the file is in a subfolder of your working directory, give its partial path, e.g. read.csv("data/STAR.csv") We are going to use the function read.csv(), which takes a file path for its first argument. ?read.csv() STAR <- read.csv("STAR.csv") # reads STAR.csv from your working directory R project to organize our workflow File > New Project... If you name your data set dat, you should call upon the object dat whenever you want to use that object. dat <- read.csv("STAR.csv") class(dat$reading) Checking code before submission Before submitting your code, clear your workspace and restart an R session. Removing objects using rm() rm() is a function that accepts two types of arguments, the objects to be removed, as names (unquoted) or character strings (quoted) list – a character vector (or NULL) naming objects to be removed Method 1 If you want to remove one object, you can use the function rm() and insert the object name as the argument. For example, rm(dat) Method 2 If your environment is cluttered and you want to clear everything in your environment you can use the function rm(list = ls()) # ls() is a function that outputs all object names in the environment Restarting R sessions and clearing workspace When you are working on something new, you should always restart your R session and clear your workspace. rm(list=ls()) Start a new R session by going to Session > Restart R Note: Depending on your default setting, restarting R session may not clear your environment. How could we not show the NAs? Use filter() to keep only the people who answered, then pipe the result into ggplot(). is.na() is TRUE when a value is missing, so is.na(ces$born_canada) == FALSE keeps the rows that are not missing. Adding na.rm=TRUE to geom_bar() does not remove the NA bar. The NAs have to be removed from the data first. ces |> filter(is.na(ces$born_canada) == FALSE) |> # keep people who are not NA for born_canada ggplot(aes(x=born_canada)) + geom_bar() This is the same is.na() we used with table() last week to count missing values: table(is.na(ces$born_canada)) ## ## FALSE TRUE ## 20048 132 Now lets try another variable, Union: ggplot(ces, aes(x=union)) + geom_bar() Wait! Something is wrong! 5.3 Factors A factor is R’s data type for categories. Similar to character, but has levels with an order. Order can be arbitrary (province), or meaningful (agree/disagree). R assumes all letters/words are character and all numbers are numeric Use factor() to turn a variable into a factor. Why? When numbers or characters are really categories. Numbers that are really categories The variable union asks “Do you belong to a union?”. It is coded 1 = yes and 0 = no. The numbers are just labels for two categories, so union is a nominal variable, or maybe ordinal. But R stores it as a number. class(ces$union) ## [1] "integer" Because union is a number, ggplot() treats it as continuous. This boxplot is wrong: it draws one box instead of one box for each group. ggplot(ces, aes(x=union, y=ndp_rating)) + geom_boxplot() Notice the x axis: 0.25, 0.50, 0.75. R thinks union could be any number between 0 and 1. The warning message about a “continuous x aesthetic” is also a sign that something is wrong. Wrapping the variable in factor() tells R that it is a category, but only temporarily. class(factor(ces$union)) ## [1] "factor" We use mutate() to save the factor as a new column, union_factor. The original union column stays the same. Now we can use union_factor in every plot without wrapping it in factor() each time. ces <- ces |> mutate(union_factor = factor(union)) class(ces$union_factor) ## [1] "factor" ggplot(ces, aes(x=union_factor, y=ndp_rating)) + geom_boxplot() Now there is one box for non-members (0), one for union members (1), and one for people who did not answer (NA). Setting the order of categories Look at another variable: born_canada Text categories are sorted alphabetically, so “Born elsewhere” comes before “Born in Canada”. ggplot(ces, aes(x=born_canada, y=con_rating)) + geom_boxplot() The levels argument of factor() sets the order ourselves. Write the categories exactly as they appear in the data. Like with union, we use mutate() to save it as a new column, born_canada_order. ces <- ces |> mutate(born_canada_order = factor(born_canada, levels=c("Born in Canada","Born elsewhere"))) ggplot(ces, aes(x=born_canada_order, y=con_rating)) + geom_boxplot() This only changes the order of the categories. The original born_canada column stays the same. Now write some code to change the union categories to words instead of 0 and 1, then make a boxplot 5.4 Canadian Election Study data We use the same 2025 Canadian Election Study (CES) data as last week. Stephenson, Laura B., Allison Harell, and Daniel Rubenson. 2025 Canadian Election Study (CES). [dataset] These are the variables we use today: variable desc. born_canada Where the respondent was born: “Born in Canada” or “Born elsewhere” union Do you belong to a union? (1 = yes, 0 = no) con_rating How do you feel about the Conservative Party? (0 = really dislike, 100 = really like) ndp_rating How do you feel about the NDP? (0 = really dislike, 100 = really like) Today we compare two groups: people born in Canada and people born elsewhere. Do they feel differently about the parties? This is a comparison, not an experiment. In an experiment, the researcher randomly decides who gets the treatment, so the groups are alike in every other way. Nobody randomly decided where our respondents were born. People born in Canada and people born elsewhere also differ in other ways (for example age, province or religion). So a difference between the groups does not show that where you were born causes the difference. Outcome 1: Conservative Party rating t.test(con_rating ~ born_canada, data = ces) ## ## Welch Two Sample t-test ## ## data: con_rating by born_canada ## t = 14.667, df = 5493.8, p-value < 2.2e-16 ## alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group Born elsewhere and group Born in Canada is not equal to 0 ## 95 percent confidence interval: ## 7.874084 10.303821 ## sample estimates: ## mean in group Born elsewhere mean in group Born in Canada ## 51.10868 42.01972 This output shows the mean of each group and a confidence interval, but it does not show the difference itself. The p-value is also hard to read (< 2.2e-16 is a very small number). Making the output easier to read – model_parameters() The function model_parameters() from the package parameters turns the t-test output into a clear table. We pipe the t-test into it. the table is actually a tiny one row dataframe, with each number as a column t.test(con_rating ~ born_canada, data = ces) |> model_parameters() ## Welch Two Sample t-test ## ## Parameter | Group | born_canada = Born elsewhere ## ------------------------------------------------------- ## con_rating | born_canada | 51.11 ## ## Parameter | born_canada = Born in Canada | Difference | 95% CI ## ---------------------------------------------------------------------- ## con_rating | 42.02 | 9.09 | [7.87, 10.30] ## ## Parameter | t(5493.83) | p ## -------------------------------- ## con_rating | 14.67 | < .001 ## ## Alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group Born elsewhere and group Born in Canada is not equal to 0 The table shows the mean of each group, the Difference, its 95% confidence interval (95% CI) and the p-value (p). Be careful of the direction of the difference. t.test() takes the mean of the first group minus the mean of the second group. The groups are in numerical order, or alphabetical order if they are text. So here it is “Born elsewhere” minus “Born in Canada”: 51.11 - 42.02 = 9.09. Interpreting the difference Respondents born elsewhere rate the Conservative Party 9 points higher (on a 0-100 scale) than respondents born in Canada. The difference is statistically significant (p < .001), so the correlation very likely isn’t due to chance. This is not an experiment, so we can’t say that being born outside Canada causes people to like the Conservatives more. An alternative explaination would be… Outcome 2: NDP rating t.test(ndp_rating ~ born_canada, data = ces) |> model_parameters() ## Welch Two Sample t-test ## ## Parameter | Group | born_canada = Born elsewhere ## ------------------------------------------------------- ## ndp_rating | born_canada | 43.35 ## ## Parameter | born_canada = Born in Canada | Difference | 95% CI ## ---------------------------------------------------------------------- ## ndp_rating | 43.81 | -0.46 | [-1.54, 0.62] ## ## Parameter | t(5303.46) | p ## ------------------------------- ## ndp_rating | -0.84 | 0.401 ## ## Alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group Born elsewhere and group Born in Canada is not equal to 0 Respondents born elsewhere rate the NDP 0.46 points lower than respondents born in Canada. The difference is not statistically significant (p = 0.401), and the confidence interval includes 0. 5.6 Visualizing differences in means Estimates and confidence intervals – geom_pointrange() The output of model_parameters() is a data frame, so we can pipe it straight into ggplot(). Because the estimate is one-dimensional (you only need either x or y), the other dimension can be used as a name label instead of a variable. In this code, y=Difference is the estimate. x=“Conservative rating” is just an axis label, so it is in quotes. t.test(con_rating ~ born_canada, data = ces) |> model_parameters() |> ggplot(aes(y=Difference,x="Conservative rating")) + geom_pointrange(aes(ymax=CI_high,ymin=CI_low)) geom_pointrange() syntax (do not run the following code) ggplot(<name of dataframe>, aes(y = Difference, # from the model_parameters() output x = "name of x-axis label")) + # x will be the x-axis label geom_pointrange(aes(ymax=CI_high,ymin=CI_low)) # from the model_parameters() output To highlight whether the difference is statistically significant, we usually add the 0-intercept line t.test(con_rating ~ born_canada, data = ces) |> model_parameters() |> ggplot(aes(y=Difference,x="Conservative rating")) + geom_pointrange(aes(ymax=CI_high,ymin=CI_low)) + geom_hline(aes(yintercept=0),linetype="dashed") # this adds a horizontal line To beautify the graph, we might change its theme and change x and y labels (xlab and ylab). Put the direction of the difference in the label, so readers know which group is higher. t.test(con_rating ~ born_canada, data = ces) |> model_parameters() |> ggplot(aes(y=Difference,x="Conservative rating")) + geom_pointrange(aes(ymax=CI_high,ymin=CI_low)) + geom_hline(aes(yintercept=0),linetype="dashed") + theme_bw() + # black and white theme xlab("") + # hides the x label ylab("Difference in means (Born elsewhere - Born in Canada)") # replaces the y label The same plot for the NDP rating. Here the confidence interval crosses the dashed 0 line, so the difference is not statistically significant. t.test(ndp_rating ~ born_canada, data = ces) |> model_parameters() |> ggplot(aes(y=Difference,x="NDP rating")) + geom_pointrange(aes(ymax=CI_high,ymin=CI_low)) + geom_hline(aes(yintercept=0),linetype="dashed") + theme_bw() + xlab("") + ylab("Difference in means (Born elsewhere - Born in Canada)") You could also flip the x and y. t.test(ndp_rating ~ born_canada, data = ces) |> model_parameters() |> ggplot(aes(x=Difference,y="NDP rating")) + geom_pointrange(aes(xmax=CI_high,xmin=CI_low)) + geom_vline(aes(xintercept=0),linetype="dashed") + theme_bw() + ylab("") + xlab("Difference in means (Born elsewhere - Born in Canada)") 5.7 Linear regression Load a different dataset (some variables from Varieties of Democracies data set) vdem <- read.csv("vdem_w6tutorial.csv") Each row is a country in 2023 (179 countries). Variables from Varieties of Democracy dataset Power distributed by gender (C) (v2pepwrgen): Q. Is political power distributed according to gender? (0: Men have a near-monopoly on political power, 4: Men and women have roughly equal political power.) Female journalists (C) (v2mefemjrn): Q. Please estimate the percentage (%) of journalists in the print and broadcast media who are women. (Interval) V-Dem codebook More details on codebook next week! From ordinal to interval The (C) means the variable is coded by country experts. Each expert answers the question on the 0 to 4 scale above. That answer is ordinal: the categories have an order, but the gaps between them are not equal. V-Dem then combines the answers of all the experts for a country into one score. This score is not limited to 0, 1, 2, 3 or 4. It can be any number, including decimals and negative numbers. Higher numbers still mean more equal power between men and women. Because it is a continuous number, we can treat it as an interval variable. summary(vdem$v2pepwrgen) ## Min. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max. ## -2.8170 0.3645 1.0180 0.9792 1.6885 3.7120 Notice the minimum is below 0 and the maximum is above 3. These are not the 0 to 4 answers from the codebook. Bivariate relationship using a scatter plot geom_point() Do countries with more women journalists also have more equal political power between men and women? vdem |> ggplot(aes(y=v2pepwrgen,x=v2mefemjrn)) + geom_point() + theme_classic() What does a regression do? A linear regression finds the straight line that best fits the points. The gap between a country’s real value and its predicted value is the error (the grey lines). Some countries are above the line and some are below. The regression line is the line that makes these errors as small as possible overall. Running a regression – lm() lm() stands for “linear model”. It uses the same ~ format as t.test(): the dependent variable goes on the left and the independent variable on the right. Like t.test(), it leaves out NAs automatically. lm() syntax (do not run the following code) lm(dependent variable ~ independent variable, data = <name of dataframe>) We save the regression as an object and use model_parameters() to make the output easy to read, just like with the t-test. journalists_model <- lm(v2pepwrgen ~ v2mefemjrn, data = vdem) journalists_model |> model_parameters() ## Parameter | Coefficient | SE | 95% CI | t(177) | p ## ----------------------------------------------------------------------- ## (Intercept) | -1.26 | 0.28 | [-1.81, -0.71] | -4.52 | < .001 ## v2mefemjrn | 0.05 | 6.36e-03 | [ 0.04, 0.07] | 8.35 | < .001 The table has two rows: v2mefemjrn: the coefficient, or slope, of the line. This is the number we care about. (Intercept): the predicted value of the dependent variable when the independent variable is 0. Not useful. Interpreting the coefficient The coefficient is interpreted as… The relationship is statistically significant (p < .001), and the confidence interval (0.04 to 0.07) does not include 0. This is not an experiment, so it does not show that women journalists cause more equal power. Other things, like wealth or democracy, could explain both. Visualizing regression line using geom_smooth() geom_smooth(method="lm") runs the same regression and draws the line. The grey band around the line is the 95% confidence interval. vdem |> ggplot(aes(y=v2pepwrgen,x=v2mefemjrn)) + geom_point(alpha=0.5) + # alpha changes the transparency of the points geom_smooth(method="lm") + # lm = linear model theme_classic() 5.8 Credits This lesson uses data from Stephenson, Laura B., Allison Harell, and Daniel Rubenson. 2025 Canadian Election Study (CES).
